A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SVL, sharing its main framework and most experiments. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated or renamed material can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot classification, downstream recognition, captioning, and ablation results in Section 5, plus qualitative outputs in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original SVL experiments and adds runtime/memory measurements, Synthia 4D segmentation, and discretization and CLIP-size experiments in Appendix A.

M1.justification: MTA and the basic backbone framework remain. v2 replaces Rep-VLI’s softmax output with an argmax over accumulated weighted spikes and moves the spiking nonlinearity after value aggregation in PointFormer attention. PointFormer itself already appeared in v1 Appendix B; its promotion and renaming are not a new architecture by themselves.

E1.justification: v2 adds Synthia 4D temporal scene segmentation, including evaluation on held-out driving sequences and weather conditions. This extends the existing scene-segmentation and temporal-recognition coverage while retaining the earlier datasets and tasks. The expanded point-text training description concerns already-present multimodal instruction-following coverage.

E2.justification: The comparative evidence expands substantially: v2 adds Spike Point Transformer to classification comparisons, KPConv, 3DShapeNets, and E-3DANN-S to the backbone comparison, and 3D/4D MinkNet14 and a matched ANN to Synthia 4D evaluation. Appendix A also compares runtime against several Spike Point Transformer configurations. Earlier comparator sets are largely retained.

E3.justification: Reported DVS Action/Gesture batch sizes change from 4096/1024 in v1 Table 12 to 64/64 in v2 Table 16; unchanged scores do not establish rerunning. New experiments introduce runtime/memory comparisons, Synthia sequence/weather splits and temporal configurations, CLIP-size and discretization sweeps, smaller PointFormer configurations, and a SpikeLLM captioning configuration.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix A adds substantial analyses of runtime/memory efficiency, temporal extent and pretraining on Synthia 4D, voxel resolution, point density, and CLIP image-encoder size. These examine efficiency and generalization factors beyond v1’s retained MTA-loss and timestep/firing-bit ablations. The qualitative examples are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run/seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including PointFormer-L+SVL classification at 93.9%/83.4%, Synthia 4D segmentation at 80.05 mIoU, runtime/memory measurements, and additional captioning configurations. These are newly reported settings, not same-setting gains over v1. The retained Pointformer ANN baseline’s energy changes from 5.1 to 30.1 mJ in Table 3; most original scores and both original ablation tables remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The attention definition changes from SN(Qs Ks^T) Vs in v1 Equation 16 to SN((Qs Ks^T) Vs) in v2 Equation 16, which also states the alternative associative evaluation order. This changes nonlinear placement rather than merely notation. The backpropagation and energy derivations are retained, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: v2 adds an independent architectural contribution to the abstract, introduction, and conclusion: the claimed first fully spike-driven point Transformer, with addition-based attention enabling faster, more efficient training. v1 presented PointFormer as a backbone without this central novelty claim. The principal SVL alignment, transfer, and efficiency claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds focused interpretations linking voxel-resolution effects to geometric fragmentation or lost structure, point-density results to diminishing returns, and larger CLIP teachers to richer semantics without additional inference cost. It also interprets temporal accumulation and runtime results. The main efficiency/generalization interpretation and the limitation concerning larger model scales remain broadly unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies two-stage multimodal-training hyperparameters and sample counts in Table 17, plus Synthia construction, splits, augmentation, and training details. These expand documentation without establishing changes to the earlier multimodal training. DVS warmup and the specific frozen text-encoder disclosure disappear. The code link is unchanged; new sample-count descriptions are internally inconsistent.

R1.justification: Beyond bibliography updates, v2 Section 2 introduces a substantive novelty argument against prior Spike Point Transformer work, criticizing its non-spiking operators and temporal encoding while positioning PointFormer as a fully spike-driven alternative. It also expands citations to SpikeLLM, KPConv, Synthia, and newer multimodal work, while removing several CLIP-background references.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, Rep-VLI explanation, parts of related work, timestep discussion, and conclusion. It promotes backbone material into Section 4.4, removes the CLIP primer, and extensively reorders the appendices around new experiments. The title, author information, acknowledgements, and impact statement also change.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references from single-column to two-column layout, substantially reflowing tables and shrinking the dialogue figure. It adds a PointFormer architecture diagram and several experimental tables, expands existing comparison tables, and redraws the retained multimodal schematic as Figure 4. These are broad display changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: The new runtime/memory comparisons and discretization and CLIP-size analyses better substantiate and qualify efficiency and transfer claims; Synthia 4D adds temporal validation. These gains are limited by missing GPU/timing details and inconsistent multimodal-training counts between Table 17 and Appendix F. The additional evidence therefore supports a modest net improvement.
